properties.title: Large Power Transformer shortage — 80% imported, 2-3 year lead times
properties.one_line: 80% of large power transformers are imported. Lead times went from months to 2-3 years. 70% of the fleet is 25+ years old. FERC identified 30 critical units whose loss in combinations of 9 could cause coast-to-coast blackout.
properties.dependency: 80% of US large power transformers imported (Canada, Mexico, South Korea, Germany, China). Lead times: 80-210 weeks (avg 120-128), up from 50 weeks in 2021. Demand up 119% since 2019. Wood Mackenzie projects 30% shortfall in 2025, 47% for generator step-up units.
properties.consequence: Average fleet age: 40 years (end of expected life). 70% are 25+ years old. FERC identified 30 critical transformers — loss of just 9 in various combinations could cause cascading coast-to-coast blackout. Each unit weighs up to 400 tons, requires custom engineering. If damaged, replacement takes months to years.
properties.who_controls: Global manufacturers (Hitachi Energy, Siemens, ABB, Hyundai). US has limited domestic manufacturing. DPA invoked June 2022 but only $254M of $500M allocated. New plants (Hitachi $457M in Virginia, Siemens $150M in Charlotte) won't be operational until 2028.
properties.mitigation: Biden invoked Defense Production Act (June 2022) for transformers. $254M allocated of $500M authorized. Hitachi announced $1B manufacturing investment. But new capacity is years away and demand continues to outpace supply.

properties.title: Grain-Oriented Electrical Steel — China produces 56%, US has one plant
properties.affected_scope: Global transformer manufacturing; US grid indirectly
properties.one_line: You can't build a transformer without GOES. China makes 56% of it. The US has one plant (AK Steel, Pennsylvania) that can't produce the highest grades. The bottleneck behind the bottleneck.
properties.dependency: Grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) is the core magnetic material in every power transformer. China produces 56% globally (Baosteel alone: 500K tonnes/year). Top 10 producers control >70% of market. US has one domestic supplier (AK Steel, PA) that doesn't produce the highest grades needed for large transformers. 80% of GOES for US transformer production is imported.
properties.consequence: GOES shortage constrains transformer manufacturing regardless of factory capacity. Even new US transformer plants (Hitachi, Siemens) will depend on imported GOES. This is the raw material dependency behind the equipment dependency behind the grid dependency.
properties.who_controls: China (56% via Baosteel, WISCO). Japan (JFE Steel, NIPPON Steel). South Korea (POSCO). Russia (NLMK). Germany (ThyssenKrupp). NIAC flagged foreign GOES dependence as national security risk.
properties.mitigation: Limited. No announced US GOES expansion to highest-grade production. Even as transformer manufacturing reshores, the raw material remains concentrated offshore.

properties.title: Puerto Rico — 11 months to restore power, then it happened again
properties.one_line: Hurricane Maria destroyed 293 substations and 2,478 miles of transmission. It took 328 days to restore power. Five years later, Hurricane Fiona knocked it all out again. No spare transformer capacity exists in the Caribbean.
properties.dependency: 2,478 miles of transmission lines, 293 substations, 31,446 miles of overhead lines damaged/destroyed. No spare large transformer capacity in the Caribbean region. Multi-year lead times meant multi-year recovery. Federal funding ($9.6B) announced 3 years after the hurricane.
properties.consequence: 328 days (11 months) to restore all customers. Largest blackout in US history. $100B in estimated infrastructure repair costs. Five years later (Sept 2022), Hurricane Fiona knocked out 100% of grid again — 4+ weeks without power in some areas. The grid was rebuilt to the same vulnerability.
properties.who_controls: LUMA Energy (private operator since 2021). Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority (PREPA, debt-ridden predecessor). Federal government (FEMA funding, Army Corps support). Transformer manufacturers (global, multi-year lead times).
properties.mitigation: $9.6B federal funding announced Sept 2020 (3 years post-Maria). Grid modernization underway but progress characterized as 'slow.' Fundamental vulnerability — island grid with no interconnection, no spare capacity in region — remains.

properties.title: Metcalf substation — 100 rifle rounds, 17 transformers, unsolved
properties.one_line: Unknown attackers cut fiber-optic lines and fired 100+ rounds at 17 transformers in 19 minutes. $15M in damage. Unsolved 11 years later. NERC had no mandatory physical security standards for substations until after this attack.
properties.dependency: April 16, 2013. PG&E substation near San Jose. Attackers cut fiber-optic lines, then fired 100+ .30-caliber rifle rounds at 17 power transformers over 19 minutes. Radiators leaked thousands of gallons of cooling oil, causing overheating/shutdown.
properties.consequence: $15M in damage. Attack exposed that high-voltage transformers are vulnerable to intentional damage with basic weapons. Pre-2013, physical security was voluntary guidelines, not mandatory. DHS indicated attack may have been committed by 'an insider' (October 2015).
properties.who_controls: PG&E (utility). FERC ordered mandatory physical security standards after the attack (2014). But standards focus on critical substations — most remain lightly protected. Unsolved 11+ years later.
properties.mitigation: FERC ordered mandatory physical security standards for substations (2014). But enforcement scope limited to 'critical' facilities. Transformer replacement lead times (2-3 years) mean a successful attack on the right targets could cause extended regional blackouts with no rapid recovery option.

properties.title: Moore County substation attacks — 40,000 without power, unsolved
properties.one_line: Gunfire hit two Duke Energy substations, knocking out power for 40,000 customers. One death (oxygen-dependent patient). Three years later, unsolved. The transformers were radiators, not windings — if the windings had been hit, replacement could have taken years.
properties.dependency: December 3, 2022. Gunfire targeted two Duke Energy distribution substations (West End and Substation #2). Two 115kV transformers hit. Damage to radiators (not windings — if windings had been destroyed, full replacement at 2-3 year lead times).
properties.consequence: 40,000 customers lost power. Karin Zoanelli, 87, died (oxygen-dependent). Initial estimate: 4 days to restore. Attack described as 'targeted' (deliberate site selection). Demonstrated that distribution substations remain vulnerable to basic weapons.
properties.who_controls: Duke Energy (utility). FBI investigated. Three years later: unsolved, no suspects. Physical security standards exist for critical substations but distribution substations are lower priority.
properties.mitigation: Post-attack security reviews. But distribution substations are numerous and lightly protected by design. The lucky outcome (radiator damage, not winding damage) masked the full vulnerability — a winding hit would have meant months-to-years replacement.

properties.title: PJM interconnection queue — 5+ year waits, transformer bottleneck
properties.one_line: Data centers added 5-7 GW/year to PJM demand. New supply adds 2-3 GW. Interconnection queue wait: 5+ years. Transformer shortage makes it worse. Two completed Silicon Valley data centers can't operate because the transformers aren't available.
properties.dependency: Data center demand: 5-7 GW added annually. New supply: 2-3 GW annually. Gap widening. Interconnection queue: 5+ years average (was months). Transformer shortages compound the delay. PJM's December 2025 auction fell 6,625 MW short of reliability requirements — first-ever shortfall.
properties.consequence: PJM capacity prices hit $333.44/MW-day (record). $9.3B+ in socialized costs across 13 states. 67M ratepayers. Gartner: power shortages will constrain 40% of AI data centers by 2027. Two Silicon Valley data centers completed but inoperable — transformers unavailable.
properties.who_controls: PJM (market rules, queue management). Transformer manufacturers (global, multi-year backlogs). Data center developers (demand signal). FERC Order 1920 (2024) attempts transmission planning reform but implementation is years away.
properties.mitigation: FERC Order 1920 requires 20-year transmission planning. New Indio River dam for Panama Canal water. Manufacturer capacity expansion underway. But demand growth continues to outpace all mitigation — the queue gets longer, not shorter.

properties.title: China battery/inverter dominance — 70% of global supply, 43% one company
properties.affected_scope: Global grid transition to renewables; US grid indirectly
properties.one_line: China supplies 70% of global batteries and 56% of components. CATL alone holds 43% market share. The US grid's transition to renewables runs through Chinese manufacturing whether anyone planned it that way or not.
properties.dependency: China deployed 174 GWh of battery storage in 2024 (triple North America). 70% of global batteries from China. 56% of battery inputs/components. CATL: 43% global market share. BYD: 12%. Plans: 200 additional battery plants by 2030, 3,000 GWh capacity.
properties.consequence: US grid transition to renewables depends on Chinese manufacturing for grid-scale storage and inverters. No comparable domestic or allied-nation supply chain at scale. Similar dynamics to GOES for transformers — the raw material/manufacturing bottleneck behind the transition.
properties.who_controls: Chinese government (subsidies, planning, export policy). CATL, BYD, EVE Energy (manufacturers). High barriers to entry for non-Chinese competitors. US policy (IRA incentives) attempts to build domestic capacity but scale gap is enormous.
properties.mitigation: IRA domestic manufacturing incentives. Some reshoring underway. But Chinese cost advantage (vertically integrated supply chain, scale) makes competition difficult. Policy constraints (tariffs, sourcing requirements) create tension between climate goals and supply chain sovereignty.
